newsitem.title: BELGIUM: ARTEMIS MINORITY SHAREHOLDERS START ASSOCIATION.
newsitem.headline: ARTEMIS MINORITY SHAREHOLDERS START ASSOCIATION.

text.p: Minority shareholders in specialist art investment firm Artemis, worried about recent developments inside the loss-making company, have set up an association to defend their interests.
"We want information. We want to find out the exact circumstances of the firm, not only financially but managerially," Pierre Stievenart told Reuters on Thursday.

"We want to know who is running the company and if, as reported in the newspapers, there are problems between the main shareholders," he said explaining the reasons behind the creation of the Artemis Shareholders Association.

Stievenart said he had been spurred to action when he found out that six of the 13-member board of directors -- including chairman Prince Antoine de Ligne had suddenly, at the firm's annual meeting in its homebase of Luxembourg on January 24, asked that their mandates not be renewed.
There had also been reports in some Belgian newspapers that the main shareholders in Artemis had a major disagreement at the meeting.
Artemis director Adrian Eeles declined to comment on the creation of the association, the reasons for the resignations or the newspaper reports of the shareholder row.

"We are trying to sort out the future of the firm. I will be better placed to give you more information in about 10 days time," he said by telephone from London. "We are in the process of reconstituting ourselves."
Artemis was created in 1970 with the sole and unique aim of investing in first class works of art in what was then, and remained for nearly two decades, a thriving market.
The major shareholder now is Belgian Compagnie Nationale a Portefeuille (CNP) -- which is closely linked to Belgian financier Albert Frere's Groupe Bruxelles Lambert -- which holds some 30 percent.
Belgian insurer Royale Belge holds around 11 percent, German insurer Nordstern 10 percent, and Belgian holding firm Brederode 4.5 percent.
Up until 1989 Artemis did well, and its share price rose to about 4,000 Belgian francs.
But it then hit trouble after some specialist staff left, the art market went into decline and the dollar weakened.
On Wednesday its share price in Brussels hit a year low of 760 francs.

The firm has racked up major losses in the past two years -- $1.56 million in the year to the end of September 1996, and $5.24 million the previous year -- and has written down the value of its stocks of works of art by $3 million from $38.4 million in the past year alone.

Belgian newspapers have hinted that Frere's CNP is considering offloading its stake in the firm, although CNP has declined to confirm the reports and the firm's managing director was unavailable for comment on Thursday.
Eeles likewise declined to comment on the CNP speculation.
Stievenart said that if the reports were true it would be a major blow to the already weak share price and, with it, to the minority shareholders.
"We support Artemis. It was and is a good idea," he said. "But we don't want to become victims of a big shareholder battle," Stievenart said.
